summary: The Ibadi school emerged from the early Khawarij movement but rejected the most extreme doctrines of classical Khawarij, particularly the broad takfir and violence against Muslims. It is the dominant school in Oman today and has historically been present in parts of North Africa and East Africa.
overview:
The Ibadi school (Arabic: al-Ibadiyyah) takes its name from Abdullah ibn Ibad al-Murri al-Tamimi (fl. late 7th century CE), though its foundational juristic figure was Jabir ibn Zayd al-Azdi (d. c. 93 AH / 711 CE), a Tabi'i scholar from Basra who is sometimes said to have been a student of Ibn Abbas.

The Ibadis trace their origins to early Khawarij circles but insist they separated from the extremist Khawarij — the Azariqa and Najdat — who declared all non-Khawarij Muslims to be polytheists (mushrikeen) deserving death. The Ibadis rejected this mass takfir. Their position: Muslims who differ with them are not mushrikeen but 'ungrateful disbelievers' (kuffar ni'mah) or simply sinners — a significantly more moderate position.

Contemporary Ibadi scholars reject the Khawarij label entirely, arguing that their school predates the extremist Khawarij factions and has a distinct theological tradition. The matter is debated among scholars: some classical Sunni scholars treated Ibadis as a moderate Khawarij offshoot; others evaluated them more favorably given their rejection of Khawarij extremism.

In fiqh, the Ibadi school has its own distinct legal tradition drawing primarily on early Basran scholarship, preserving positions not found in the four Sunni madhabs. Ibadis pray behind Sunni Imams and Sunnis in Oman typically pray in Ibadi mosques without objection — a practical coexistence that reflects the moderate nature of the school.

Today, Ibadis are the overwhelming majority in Oman (where it is the official state religion), with smaller communities in Zanzibar (Tanzania), Libya (Jabal Nafusa), Algeria (Mzab Valley), and Tunisia (Djerba Island).

Islam.wiki covers the Ibadi school with recognition of both its historical connection to early Khawarij movements and its distinct identity as a surviving minority tradition that has evolved significantly from classical Khawarij extremism.

Classical Sunni scholars have differed on their status. Modern Ibadi scholars reject the Khawarij label. Their theological and jurisprudential positions differ from Ahl us-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah.
